extracted.intended_audience: astronomers, mathematicians, and observational scientists performing orbital computations and interpreting comet phenomena (historical/Principia readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and interpretive criteria for (a) diagnosing and explaining comet-tail phenomena and (b) correcting a graphically-determined cometary trajectory from discrete observations. Includes observational rules-of-thumb, physical interpretation, and a three-observation algebraic correction algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tails originate from the comet's head (not from atmospheric refraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pendent igitur Phænomena caudæ à motu capitis, non autem à regione coeli in qua caput conspicitur; & propterea non fiunt per refractionem coelorum, sed à capite suppeditante materiam oriuntur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational indicators: tails appear to arise from the head and follow motions related to the head; tails change with head motion and observer position. Anti-interpretation: tails are not caused by refraction of the heavens. Supporting analogy: smoke rising from a burning body rises upward (perpendicular if the body is stationary, obliquely if the body moves), similarly vapors ascend from the comet head under solar influence and retain components of the comet's prior motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tail direction, curvature, and apparent straightness relate to head motion and observer position
rubrics_metrics.description: Quod in planis orbium Cometarum per Solem transeuntibus jacentes, deviant ab oppositione Solis in eas semper partes quas capita in orbibus illis progredientia relinquunt... Quod caudæ non deviantes apparent rectæ, deviantes autem incurvantur. Quod curvatura major est ubi major est deviatio, & magis sensibilis ubi cauda cæteris paribus longior est: nam in brevioribus curvatura ægre animadvertitur. Quod deviationis angulus minor est juxta caput Cometæ, major juxta caudæ extremitatem alteram, atque adeò quod cauda convexo sui latere partes respicit à quibus fit deviatio...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation rules: (1) The tail deviates from exact antisolar direction in the sense left behind by the head's motion in its orbit. (2) A non-deviating tail appears straight; a deviating tail appears curved. (3) Curvature increases where deviation is larger and is more detectable for longer tails. (4) Deviation angle is smaller near the head and larger near the tail end; the convex side of the tail faces the side from which deviation occurs. Observational note: apparent straightness or curvature depends on the observer's position relative to the comet's orbital plane; moving the observer changes perceived deviation gradually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brightness, translucency, and inferred rarity of cometary vapors from stellar translucence
rubrics_metrics.description: Nam & caudarum insignis raritas colligitur ex astris per eas translucentibus. Atmosphæra terrestris luce Solis splendens, crassitudine sua paucorum milliarium, & astra omnia & ipsam Lunam obscurat & extinguit penitus: per immensam verò caudarum crassitudinem, luce pariter Solari illustratam, astra minima absque claritatis detrimento translucere noscuntur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: if stars are seen through a tail without appreciable dimming, the tail must be far rarer than Earth's atmosphere. Quantitative comparison: terrestrial air column arguments (ratios of densities with altitude) indicate that cometary atmospheres/comae and tails can be extremely rare yet still reflect sunlight sufficiently to be visible. Practical implication: apparent luminosity of a tail does not imply great density; translucency of stars through tails is evidence of very low particle density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric method to infer time of vapor ejection from tail terminus
rubrics_metrics.description: Quo tempore vapor à capite ad terminum caudæ ascendit, cognosci fere potest ducendo rectam à termino caudæ ad Solem, & notando locum ubi recta illa Trajectoriam secat. Nam vapor in termino caudæ, si rectà ascendat à Sole, ascendere cæpit à capite quo tempore caput erat in loco intersectionis. At vapor non rectà ascendit à Sole, sed motum Cometæ, quem ante ascensum suum habebat, retinendo, & cum motu ascensus sui eundem componendo, ascendit oblique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: draw a line from the tail's end to the Sun and find where that line intersects the comet's orbit; the time when the comet was at that intersection corresponds (for a straight ascent) to when the vapor now at the tail terminus began to ascend. Correction: because vapor ascent is composed with the comet's prior motion, ascent is generally oblique, so computed times must account for that oblique composition. Example: applied to an observed comet to infer that vapor at tail end (Jan 25) began ascending at a head position on Dec 11, consuming about 45 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish long, transient sunward-produced tails from short, persistent exhalation columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Unde etiam caudæ Cometarum aliorum quæ breves sunt, non ascendunt motu celeri & perpetuo à capitibus & mox evanescunt, sed sunt permanentes vaporum & exhalationum columnæ, à capitibus lentissimo multorum dierum motu propagatæ, quæ, participando motum illum capitum quem habuere sub initio, per coelos una cum capitibus moveri pergunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation rule: (1) Very long, rapidly produced tails near perihelion are composed of vapor that ascended quickly and may fade; (2) short tails often consist of persistent columns of vapor/exhalation propagated slowly from the head and move with the comet. Observational consequence: permanence and motion relative to the head distinguish the two kinds; the former expand greatly near the Sun, the latter maintain attachment and similar motion to the head.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms proposed for vapor ascent: rarefaction by heat and radiative action
rubrics_metrics.description: Keplerus ascribit actioni radiorum lucis materiam caudæ secum rapientium... Suspicor ascensum illum ex rarefactione materiæ caudarum potius oriri. Ascendit fumus in camino impulsu aeris cui innatat. Aer ille per calorem rarefactus ascendit, ob diminutam suam gravitatem specificam, & fumum implicatum rapit secum. Quidni cauda Cometæ ad eundem modum ascenderit à Sole? Nam radii Solares non agitant Media quæ permeant, nisi in reflexione & refractione. Particulæ reflectentes ea actione calefactæ calefacient auram ætheream cui implicantur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarized mechanisms: (a) Kepler's idea — solar rays carry matter away; (b) Newton's favored idea — solar heating rarefies the cometary atmosphere, reducing its specific gravity so it ascends and entrains reflective particles; these heated particles also illuminate the tail by reflecting sunlight. Additional outward tendency arises from bodies' gyration about the Sun. Observational implication: near-solar conditions (greater heating and rarer atmosphere) produce the largest, most luminous tails; heating of head explains observed darkening of heads during perihelion phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cometary atmospheres and long-term replenishment of planetary liquids and subtle spirits
rubrics_metrics.description: Quæ ad conservationem marium & humorum in Planetis Cometæ requiri videntur; ex quorum exhalationibus & vaporibus condensatis, quicquid liquoris per vegetationem & putrefactionem consumitur & in terram aridam convertitur, continuò suppleri & refici possit. Nam vegetabilia omnia ex liquoribus omnino crescunt, dein magna ex parte in terram aridam per putrefactionem abeunt... Porrò suspicor spiritum illum, qui aeris nostri pars minima est sed subtilissima & optima, & ad rerum omnium vitam requiritur, ex Cometis præcipue venire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis to evaluate: comet exhalations may diffusely seed planets with vapors that condense into liquids (rain, springs) and supply the subtle portion of air necessary for life. Use as explanatory criterion: if cometary vapors can be shown to dilute and mix into planetary atmospheres over time, they may account for replenishment of seas and subtle atmospheric components. This is speculative and supported by analogies to terrestrial evaporation/condensation and long-term mass transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of cometary atmosphere size relative to perihelion/aphelion (expansion and contraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Atmosphæræ Cometarum in descensu eorum in Solem excurrendo in caudas diminuuntur, & (ea certe in parte quæ Solem respicit) angustiores redduntur: & vicissim in recessu eorum à Sole, ubi jam minus excurrunt in caudas, ampliantur... Minimæ autem apparent ubi capita jam modo ad Solem calefacta in caudas maximas & fulgentissimas abiere, & nuclei fumo forsan crassiore & nigriore in Atmosphærarum partibus infimis circundantur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation rule: as a comet approaches the Sun its atmosphere tends to be driven into the tail (sunward side thinner), making the tail larger and the head possibly darker/denser; when receding, the atmosphere expands. Observational markers: minimum apparent atmospheres occur immediately after perihelion for comets that emitted maximal tails, with a darker, thicker smoke-like region near the nucleus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure (Prop. XLII) to correct a graphically-determined comet trajectory from three observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Trajectoriam Cometæ graphicè inventam corrigere. Oper. 1: Assume a position of the plane of trajectory determined graphically; select three comet positions from accurate observations maximally separated; let A be time between first and second, B time between second and third. Find the three true places in the assumed plane by trigonometric operations; then, about the Sun as umbilicum, by arithmetic operations (Prop. XXI Lib. I), describe the conic section whose areas radii to the true places bound, calling the areas D and E (D between first and second, E between second and third). Let T be the time in which area D+E would be described by the comet's velocity per Prop. XVI Lib. I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Full multi-step algorithm (summary of Oper.1–3):
- Oper.1: From three well-separated observed apparent places, compute their true positions in the assumed orbital plane via trigonometry. Compute area segments D and E subtended at the Sun by radii to these true places; obtain T, the time corresponding to area D+E using the comet's computed velocity law.
- Oper.2: Increase the assumed longitude of the nodes of the trajectory by P (20' or 30') while keeping the plane's inclination to the ecliptic fixed; recompute three true places in the new plane, the corresponding orbit and its area segments d and e, and the time t for area d+e.
- Oper.3: Instead keep the original node longitude and increase the plane's inclination by Q (20' or 30'); recompute the three true places, the orbit, corresponding area segments δ and ε, and the time τ for area δ+ε.
- Form ratios: let C:1 = A:B, G:1 = D:E, g:1 = d:e, γ:1 = δ:ε; let S be the true elapsed time between the first and third observations. Find integers m and n (with observed +/− signs) satisfying G - C = mG - mg + nG - nγ and T - S = mT - mt + nT - nτ. Then corrected inclination = I + nQ (if I was original inclination and K original node longitude, node longitude becomes K + mP). For rectum and transverse axis: if R, r, ρ are latus rectum values from the three operations and 1/L, 1/l, 1/λ their transverse reciprocals, the true latus rectum equals R + mr - mR + nρ - nR and the true transverse reciprocal equals 1/(L + ml - mL + nλ - nL). From the transverse axis follows the comet's period.

Application notes: choose three observations as widely separated as possible; P and Q perturbations are suggested small angular increments (20'–30') to probe sensitivity; m and n are integer corrections determined by comparing area/time ratios and solving the linear relations; this yields corrected orbital elements (node longitude, inclination, latus rectum, transverse axis) and the period.
